meta.title: Route vehicles, lights and audible warnings
meta.summary: You will learn when to give way to trams and buses, whether you may enter the lane for route vehicles (bus lane), which lights to switch on by day, at night and in fog, and when you may sound the horn.

p: A tram cannot drive around an obstacle and takes longer to stop than a car. So where tram tracks cross the carriageway outside an intersection, a tram has priority over all trackless vehicles ⟦19⟧.
There is one exception: when a tram is leaving the depot, this priority does not apply ⟦20⟧.

The lane for route vehicles (bus lane) is marked with signs 5.9, 5.9.2-5.9.4 and 5.10.1-5.10.3. Only public transport (under the Rules, this includes taxis) and other vehicles of category M3 may drive and stop in it. Everyone else is prohibited from driving and stopping in this lane ⟦21⟧.

Important: para. 126 was amended by Ministry of Internal Affairs Order No. 305 of 27.04.2026. The current version contains no exceptions for a lane separated by a broken line: other vehicles may no longer enter it before a turn, when joining the road, or to let passengers board or alight ⟦22⟧.
list: Under the Rules, a taxi is public transport, so it may drive and stop in this lane ⟦23⟧.

Where there is no cycle track or cycle lane, cyclists ride along the right edge of the carriageway, including in this lane, but only from the age of 14. A similar exception applies to e-scooters ⟦24⟧.
When turning right, you cross the lane for route vehicles at the intersection and give way to route vehicles and other public transport travelling in it, including taxis ⟦25⟧.
Sign 5.10.1 marks a road where the lane for route vehicles runs against the general flow of traffic. You must not move into it, for example to overtake ⟦26⟧.
lesson.tip: Turning right and crossing a lane marked with sign 5.9? Give way to route vehicles and other public transport travelling in it ⟦27⟧.

lesson.h: A bus moving off from a stop
p: In built-up areas, drivers give way to buses and trolleybuses that are running on their route and moving off from a designated stop ⟦28⟧. This makes it easier for town transport to join the traffic flow, and passengers wait less.
Note the three conditions: a built-up area, a bus or trolleybus running on its route, and a designated stop.

Outside built-up areas there is no such rule: there, a bus that is moving off and changing lanes must itself give way to vehicles travelling in the same direction ⟦29⟧. And even in town, the driver of a bus or trolleybus moves off from a stop only after making sure that others are giving way ⟦30⟧.
During the hours of darkness, in poor visibility and in tunnels, headlights are always switched on, even if the road is well lit ⟦31⟧.
Poor visibility means the road is visible for less than 300 m because of fog, rain, snowfall, dust and the like, and also at twilight ⟦32⟧.
list: On motor cars and mopeds: position lamps (side lights) plus main-beam or dipped headlights ⟦33⟧.
On bicycles: headlights or lamps. On horse-drawn carts: lamps, if fitted ⟦34⟧.
On trailers and towed vehicles: position lamps ⟦35⟧.
In a tunnel, daytime running lights are not enough: switch on the position lamps and dipped or main-beam headlights ⟦36⟧.
The hours of darkness are the period from the end of evening twilight to the beginning of morning twilight. Twilight is a condition of poor visibility, and headlights are needed then too ⟦37⟧.

p: During daylight hours, all moving vehicles must have dipped headlights or daytime running lights on. This is so that the vehicle can be seen from afar ⟦38⟧.
In daytime, you may also use the front fog lamps instead of dipped headlights ⟦39⟧.
lesson.tip: Older question collections contain the rule “dipped headlights by day only out of town”. The current version requires dipped headlights or daytime running lights on all moving vehicles ⟦40⟧.

lesson.h: When to switch from main-beam to dipped headlights
p: Main-beam headlights light up the road well but dazzle other drivers. So you switch from main-beam to dipped headlights ⟦41⟧:

Note: in a built-up area you must switch if the road is lit. On an unlit village street, main-beam headlights are allowed as long as they do not dazzle anyone. When you are being overtaken, also switch to dipped headlights so as not to dazzle the overtaking driver through their mirrors ⟦42⟧.
list: in a built-up area, if the road is lit;
when passing an oncoming vehicle - at least 150 m before it, and even earlier if its driver flashes their headlights to show that you are dazzling them;
in any other case where you could dazzle the drivers of oncoming vehicles or vehicles travelling in the same direction, for example when you are following another vehicle.
lesson.tip: Dazzled by oncoming headlights? Switch on the hazard warning lights and stop without changing lanes ⟦43⟧.

list: In poor visibility, front fog lamps may be used on their own or together with dipped or main-beam headlights ⟦44⟧.
During the hours of darkness on an unlit road: only together with dipped or main-beam headlights ⟦45⟧.
Front fog lamps may be switched on only when the position lamps are on ⟦46⟧.
Rear fog lamps: only in poor visibility. They must not be connected to the brake lights ⟦47⟧.
lesson.tip: A rear fog lamp is very bright. In clear weather it dazzles those behind you, so it is not switched on without fog, rain or snow.

lesson.h: Stopping and parking in the dark
p: If you stop during the hours of darkness on an unlit section of road, or in poor visibility, switch on the position lamps. In poor visibility, you may add dipped headlights, front fog lamps and rear fog lamps ⟦48⟧.
Position lamps not working? Move the vehicle off the road. If that is impossible, mark it in accordance with paras. 44 and 45: with the hazard warning lights and a warning triangle ⟦49⟧.

These powerful lamps may be used only outside built-up areas and only when there are no oncoming vehicles. In built-up areas, only drivers of emergency and special services on an official assignment use them ⟦50⟧.

The horn may be used in only two cases: to warn other drivers that you are going to overtake outside built-up areas, and when it is needed to prevent a road traffic accident ⟦51⟧. Sounding the horn in a traffic jam, hurrying someone who is standing still at a green light, or greeting a friend is a violation.

To warn of overtaking, you can also give a light signal: by day, briefly switch the headlights on and off several times; during the hours of darkness, switch from dipped to main-beam headlights several times ⟦52⟧.
A light signal is also given in town when you catch up with a driver moving slowly in the left lane: they must move over to the right and free the lane for the faster vehicle ⟦53⟧.
lesson.tip: In town, the horn is allowed in only one case: to prevent a road traffic accident.

p: These terms are easy to confuse. A route vehicle is a public bus, trolleybus or tram running on an established route with designated stops. Public transport is a wider term: it covers public vehicles used for regular and irregular carriage of passengers and luggage, and also taxis ⟦54⟧.
lesson.tip: Priority at a stop ⟦55⟧ belongs only to buses and trolleybuses on their route, while a taxi may also drive in the lane for route vehicles ⟦56⟧.

lesson.h: Beacons, the “Road train” sign and retroreflective marking
list: A flashing amber (orange or yellow) beacon is switched on, for example, on vehicles used in road construction, repair and cleaning, on vehicles carrying overweight loads, oversized loads or dangerous goods and on their escort vehicles, and on buses carrying organised groups of children ⟦57⟧.
The “Road train” identification sign is switched on while moving, and during the hours of darkness and in poor visibility also while stopped or parked ⟦58⟧.
The outlines of the sides and rear of vehicles of categories M2, M3, N2, N3, O2, O3 and O4 are marked with retroreflective material so that a large vehicle can be seen in headlights ⟦59⟧.

keyFacts: Outside intersections, a tram has priority over trackless vehicles, except when leaving the depot ⟦1⟧.
Only public transport (including taxis) and other vehicles of category M3 may drive and stop in the lane for route vehicles ⟦2⟧.
Since the amendments of 27.04.2026, para. 126 has no exceptions for a broken line: other vehicles may neither drive nor stop in the lane for route vehicles ⟦3⟧.
In built-up areas, give way to buses and trolleybuses moving off from a designated stop ⟦4⟧.
Hours of darkness, poor visibility, tunnel: position lamps plus dipped or main-beam headlights, even on a lit road ⟦5⟧.
Poor visibility: visibility of the road of less than 300 m in fog, rain, snowfall, dust and the like, and also at twilight ⟦6⟧.
By day, on all moving vehicles: dipped headlights or daytime running lights ⟦7⟧.
Main-beam to dipped headlights: in a lit built-up area, at least 150 m before an oncoming vehicle, and whenever you could dazzle others ⟦8⟧.
Dazzled: hazard warning lights, do not change lanes, stop ⟦9⟧.
Rear fog lamps: only in poor visibility ⟦10⟧.
Parking during the hours of darkness on an unlit section of road: with the position lamps on ⟦11⟧.
The horn: only to warn of overtaking outside built-up areas and to prevent a road traffic accident ⟦12⟧.
mistakes: “Headlights are needed by day only out of town”. Under the current version, all moving vehicles must have dipped headlights or daytime running lights on during daylight hours ⟦13⟧.

Using the lane for route vehicles to get around a traffic jam, or entering it to drop off a passenger. Only public transport (including taxis) and other vehicles of category M3 may drive and stop in it ⟦14⟧.
Switching to dipped headlights only when the oncoming vehicle is already very close. You must do it at least 150 m before it ⟦15⟧.
Switching on the rear fog lamps on a clear night. They are used only in poor visibility ⟦16⟧.
Sounding the horn in town to hurry others. The horn is allowed only to prevent a road traffic accident and to warn of overtaking outside built-up areas ⟦17⟧.
Swerving sharply when dazzled by oncoming headlights. The right way: hazard warning lights, stay in your lane and stop ⟦18⟧.
